name: Economic liberalism
summary: Economic liberalism holds that an economy should be organised through private property, contract and competitive markets, with the state limited to protecting property, enforcing contracts and supplying a few public goods. It favours free trade, restrained taxation and spending, and opposes protectionism, central planning and most state direction of investment. Strands differ on how far the state should provide a safety net, from classical and libertarian minimalism to the social market and ordoliberal view.

sources.usedFor: Reference entry on economic liberalism: laissez-faire, attacks on monopolies and guild restrictions, occupational freedom, free trade, Smith.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Smith named protecting society from other societies' violence, by a military force, as the sovereign's first duty.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: Britannica describes the classical-liberal exchange economy as based on the division of labour, which Smith made the source of wealth.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: Britannica says classical liberals hold that government must provide law enforcement, and Smith made the administration of justice a duty of the sovereign.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Smith held that the enormous public debts of European nations oppress and will probably ruin them, a view that tells against running deficits.

ban-cartels.rationale: Simons's programme of liberal economic policy makes the elimination of private monopoly its first and indispensable proposal, with persistent prosecution of producers who organise for price maintenance or output limitation and restraint of trade treated as a major crime (Part I, the five proposals).

ban-interest.rationale: Smith held that a law prohibiting interest altogether does not prevent it and only raises the cost of borrowing by adding the risk of evading the law (Book II, ch. 4, Of Stock Lent at Interest).

bound-labor.rationale: Smith held that hindering a poor man from employing his strength where he chooses is a plain violation of the most sacred property, his own labour.

central-planning.rationale: Britannica says Hayek demonstrated that a centrally planned economy is impossible, as part of the classical-liberal revival.

country-wealth-only-from-land.rationale: Smith examined the agricultural systems of political economy and judged their notion that only labour employed upon land is productive too narrow and confined, rejecting their claim that manufacturing labour adds nothing (Book IV, ch. 9).

cut-consumption-tax.rationale: Smith held that taxes on the necessaries of life raise the wages of labour and fall finally on landlords and rich consumers with an over-charge, so that the middling and superior ranks ought always to oppose them (Book V, ch. 2, Taxes upon Consumable Commodities).

economic-freedom.rationale: Britannica reports Hayek's argument in The Road to Serfdom that interventionist measures lead inevitably to totalitarianism.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Smith attacked England's monopoly of the colony trade and the exclusive-trade system as costly to the ruling country, and Britannica reports classical liberals opposing mercantilist restrictions.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Britannica says classical liberalism holds individual rights to be supreme and inherent in each person, with freedom limited only by others' equal freedom, under known laws applied to all.

extrajudicial-killing.rationale: Britannica makes the rule of law, with known laws instead of arbitrary decisions, crucial to the classical-liberal limit on government.

free-trade.rationale: Smith's Wealth of Nations champions the liberal system of free exportation and importation, and Britannica reports that free trade benefits all parties on his argument.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Britannica says classical economics rested on belief in the superiority of a self-regulating market.

moral-incentives.rationale: Britannica says that on the classical-liberal view self-interest in an exchange economy serves the group.

national-church-status.rationale: Smith argued that endowed established clergy grow indolent and that equal treatment of many sects would keep religious zeal harmless, which tells against a special legal status for one church.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Smith gave the sovereign a third duty of public works and institutions beyond defence and justice, and Britannica says classical liberals accepted education and sanitation; the night-watchman limit is the view of dissenters such as Spencer and Sumner.

no-business-privileges.rationale: Smith condemned the monopolizing spirit of merchants and exclusive privileges of trading companies, and Britannica says private monopoly leads to exploitation and stagnation.

occupational-licensing.rationale: The entry presents economic liberalism as attacking guild restrictions and monopolies that violate people's natural liberty of seeking their livelihoods (de la Court) and Smith's call to end restraints on free movement of labour, which favours open entry to trades, though it does not mention modern licensing as such.

positive-liberty.rationale: Britannica says classical-tradition liberals hold that government should only protect freedom, while the view that government should remove poverty and ignorance as obstacles is modern liberalism's.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: Smith held that the unrestrained freedom of the corn trade is the best remedy for dearth and that famines come from government's attempts to remedy it.

private-courts-defense.rationale: Smith made establishing an exact administration of justice a duty of the sovereign, paid for by the society, not something to leave to private firms.

production-for-use.rationale: Britannica describes the market, with prices set by buyers and sellers, as what decides what is produced, in place of production planned to meet needs.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Britannica says individuals are to be governed by known laws.

property-fundamental.rationale: Smith called the property a man has in his own labour the most sacred and inviolable, and Britannica gives government the role of protecting individual rights as supreme.

public-ownership.rationale: Britannica reports Smith's view that state control of the economy leads to regimentation, exploitation and stagnation, where a free market serves the public good.

self-ownership.rationale: Britannica states that classical liberalism embraces self-ownership: each individual has control over their choices, actions and body.

separated-powers.rationale: Britannica lists the separation of powers among the political ideals classical liberalism advocated.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Britannica calls the rule of law crucial, with individuals governed by known laws and not arbitrary decisions,.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Smith said a statesman who tried to direct how private people employ their capitals would assume an authority that no person or council could safely hold.

state-harmful.rationale: Britannica says all classical liberals hold that government is necessary to protect individuals from being harmed by others, so abolishing the state contradicts the doctrine.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Smith held that restraints on importing what can be made at home are useless or hurtful, and Britannica lists ending protective tariffs among classical-liberal demands.

taxation-theft.rationale: Smith held that the sovereign's duties are properly paid for by the general contribution of the society and set out maxims for taxes, so taxation as such is not theft.

total-state.rationale: Britannica reports the classical-liberal principle of limiting the power of government, and Hayek argued, on Britannica's account, that redistributive intervention leads to totalitarianism.

trade-surplus.rationale: Smith called the whole doctrine of the balance of trade absurd, the doctrine that a country gains by exporting more than it imports.

missingStatements.text: Prices in a market should be set by buyers and sellers, not by the government.
missingStatements.rationale: Smith and Hayek hold that prices carry dispersed information and that fixing them causes shortages or waste, a defining position beyond emergency food prices.

missingStatements.text: The state's main economic role is to protect property and enforce contracts, not to direct the economy.
missingStatements.rationale: Described as the basis of the ideology: a strong state protecting property rights and contracts without planning.
missingStatements.declined: Covered by night-watchman-state, which this audit answers 0 because adherents split on how narrow the state role is; the proposal would be a duplicate.

missingStatements.text: Governments should balance their budgets and keep public debt low.
missingStatements.rationale: Wikipedia lists restrained fiscal policy and minimal public debt as common positions; existing statements cover only stimulus deficits.

evidence.quote: Adam Smith's The Wealth of Nations (1776) argued that free markets enhance overall welfare, with self-seeking individuals inadvertently serving the public good through the price mechanism.
Classical liberalism's economic views, influenced by Adam Smith 's The Wealth of Nations , support free markets and minimal government intervention, fostering competition, and lower prices.

scope: Economic liberalism as the defining sources present it: the view that economic life is best ordered by private property, free competition, free trade and laissez faire with the state kept to a narrow role (Levy, Economic Liberalism, Introduction: a system of thought from the seventeenth century, not only the nineteenth-century free-trade school; Britannica on classical-liberal economic thought). Centred on the classical tradition of Adam Smith and his descendants. Excludes the broader political liberalism of rights and constitutions, neoliberalism as a distinct doctrine, and modern social liberalism, except where the sources name them as the same position.
